id: More than one man has reached up my skirt

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’ve stopped asking: ¿Why? I’ve let a man whistle from the table for more beer, & brought it to him with a smile. I’ve slapped a man & ran while he laughed — atrevida. I’ve had a miscarriage. I’ve let a man kiss me after an abortion & comforted his hot tears. I’ve done these things, while other girls work in maquilas piecing together Dell computer boards, while other girls work in brothels, & cake foundation across their bruised arms, while other girls ride the bus home alone at night, every night, while other girls are found wearing clothes that don’t belong to them, or no clothes at all. I’ve done all of this while other girls are found with puta written in blood across their broken bellies. My mother used to cover my eyes when we’d walk by girls working the corner, & say: See how lucky you are,not to have to work like they do? I have been muy puta, have been called puta.Yes, I’d say, very lucky.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Why, Dell, See

outputs.L1:
I’ve stopped asking, ¿Why? I’ve let a man whistle from the table for more beer and brought it to him with a smile. I’ve slapped a man and run while he laughed—atrevida. I’ve had a miscarriage. I’ve let a man kiss me after an abortion and comforted his hot tears.

I’ve done these things while other girls work in maquilas, piecing together Dell computer boards; while other girls work in brothels and cake foundation across their bruised arms; while other girls ride the bus home alone at night, every night; while other girls are found wearing clothes that don’t belong to them, or no clothes at all. I’ve done all of this while other girls are found with puta written in blood across their broken bellies.

My mother used to cover my eyes when we walked past girls working the corner and say, “See how lucky you are, not to have to work like they do?”

I have been muy puta. I have been called puta.

“Yes,” I’d say. “Very lucky.”
outputs.L2:
I no longer ask, “¿Why?” When a man at a table summoned me with a whistle for another beer, I served him smiling. I struck a man and fled as he laughed and called me atrevida. I miscarried. After an abortion, I allowed a man to kiss me, then soothed him as his burning tears fell.

All this happened while other girls assembled Dell circuit boards in maquilas; while others worked in brothels, hiding the bruises on their arms beneath thick foundation; while girls traveled home alone by bus night after night; while some were discovered in someone else’s clothing—or with nothing on at all. I did these things as other girls were found with puta scrawled in blood over their shattered stomachs.

Whenever my mother and I passed girls working a street corner, she would shield my eyes and tell me, “Look how fortunate you are that you don’t have to earn a living the way they do.”

I have been muy puta. I have been named puta.

“Yes,” I would answer. “So fortunate.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker recounts deeply personal experiences of sexism, defiance, miscarriage, abortion, and emotional vulnerability. Her story is not presented in isolation; rather, it unfolds alongside the exploitation of girls and women in factories, brothels, and unsafe public spaces. By placing these experiences side by side, the text connects individual pain to broader systems of gendered oppression and economic inequality.

The text also confronts the brutal violence inflicted on women, emphasizing how victims are often shamed, blamed, and dehumanized—even after death. This treatment reveals a culture that not only fails to protect women but also judges them for the violence committed against them. The speaker’s mother underscores the role of privilege by describing distance from sex work as a form of protection. Her perspective suggests that avoiding exploitation is not simply a matter of personal virtue or choice, but may depend on social, economic, and familial circumstances.

When the speaker acknowledges that she herself has been labeled “puta,” she exposes the hypocrisy behind such judgments. The term is used to police, humiliate, and reduce women regardless of their actual experiences. At the same time, the speaker remains aware of her relative privilege: although she has been stigmatized, she recognizes that she has not faced the same degree of exploitation or danger as many other women. This tension allows the text to criticize misogynistic labeling while also reflecting honestly on differences in vulnerability, protection, and social position.
outputs.L4:
The speaker explores gendered violence, sexual stigma, and the precariousness of womanhood by placing her own intimate experiences alongside the exploitation and murder of women who work in maquilas, brothels, and on the streets. This juxtaposition connects forms of harm that might otherwise appear separate: private humiliation, sexual judgment, economic exploitation, and lethal violence. Her personal story is therefore not presented as an isolated experience, but as part of a broader social order in which women’s bodies are controlled, classified, and made vulnerable.

The repeated use of the word “puta” is central to this critique. The insult reduces women to a sexual label and suggests that any departure from prescribed feminine behavior can be used to justify contempt or abuse. Although the speaker may appear to possess greater social or economic privilege than the women she invokes, the label exposes how unstable that privilege is. Respectability offers only conditional protection, because misogyny can quickly strip any woman of social legitimacy by portraying her as sexually improper.

At the same time, the text does not erase the significant differences among women’s circumstances. Those employed in factories or the sex trade, as well as women surviving in public spaces, face intensified dangers created by poverty, labor exploitation, and institutional neglect. By bringing these women into the same frame as her own experience, the speaker reveals a continuum of gendered violence. Verbal degradation and intimate mistreatment exist within the same patriarchal culture that treats marginalized women as disposable and allows their disappearances and murders to go unpunished.

The speaker’s identification with stigmatized women thus becomes both personal and political. Her repeated labeling as “puta” demonstrates that womanhood itself is precarious under misogyny: safety and respect depend on conforming to restrictive expectations, and even apparent privilege cannot guarantee protection. Through this comparison, the text condemns a social system that ranks women according to class, occupation, and sexual reputation while exposing all of them to judgment, exploitation, and violence.

### Why Choose Dell? See the Difference

Why do so many people choose Dell for their technology needs? The answer lies in the company’s combination of reliable performance, practical design, and extensive customer support. From lightweight laptops for students to powerful workstations for professionals, Dell offers devices for nearly every type of user.

See how Dell continues to adapt through energy-efficient products, modern security features, and customizable configurations. Whether you need a computer for work, gaming, or everyday use, Dell provides flexible options designed to balance quality, performance, and price.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person prose poem in Spanglish about womanhood, sexuality, guilt, and the violence faced by women in Ciudad Juárez, using repetition and the word “puta” as a recurring motif.
counterfactuals.output:
Me llamaron **puta** antes de que yo supiera  
que mi cuerpo tenía puertas,  
antes de aprender que una puerta abierta  
no es una invitación,  
que una falda no firma contratos,  
que decir sí una vez no significa siempre.

**Puta**, dijeron, porque caminé sola.  
**Puta**, porque caminé acompañada.  
**Puta**, porque mi boca tenía lipstick  
y también palabras.  
Porque dije *I want*.  
Porque dije *I don’t*.  
Porque dije *this body is mine*  
y el mundo respondió con una carcajada.

Cargo la culpa como una medalla oxidada.  
Mi madre me enseñó: cruza las piernas,  
baja la mirada, avisa cuando llegues.  
Mi madre me enseñó a sobrevivir  
sin llamarlo miedo.  
*Text me. Call me. Don’t take that street.*  
No tomes taxi sola.  
No confíes.  
No sonrías demasiado.  
No seas tan fría.  
No seas tan puta.

En Ciudad Juárez, el desierto guarda nombres  
debajo de la lengua.  
Nombres de muchachas que salieron de la maquila,  
que esperaban el camión,  
que llevaban sueños pequeños en la bolsa:  
una llave, un peine, unas monedas,  
the ordinary evidence of being alive.

Luego aparecen cruces rosadas  
donde debería haber cumpleaños.  
Luego aparecen madres  
pegando rostros a los postes,  
preguntándole al viento:  
*Have you seen my daughter?*  
¿La has visto?  
¿La has visto?  
¿La has visto?

Y alguien murmura **puta**,  
como si la palabra explicara una tumba,  
como si el deseo de una mujer  
fuera permiso para borrarla,  
como si la noche fuera culpable  
y no la mano,  
y no el hombre,  
y no la ciudad que aprende a no mirar.

Yo también soy esa mujer y no lo soy.  
I am the body walking home.  
I am the mother waiting beside the phone.  
Soy la hermana que memoriza placas,  
la amiga que comparte ubicación,  
la hija que miente: *ya llegué*,  
aunque todavía le falten tres cuadras  
de oscuridad.

**Puta**, digo ahora,  
y la palabra me quema menos cuando es mía.  
La saco de sus bocas,  
la lavo con saliva y rabia,  
la cuelgo de mi cuello  
como una campana de alarma.

**Puta** si deseo.  
**Puta** si sobrevivo.  
**Puta** si mi placer no pide perdón.  
Pero no cadáver.  
No silencio.  
No expediente perdido bajo otros expedientes.

I want to be a woman without instructions.  
Quiero bailar sin calcular la salida.  
Quiero besar sin confesarme después.  
Quiero que ninguna madre aprenda  
a reconocer a su hija por la ropa.

Me llamaron **puta**  
para hacerme pequeña.

Yo repito **puta, puta, puta**  
hasta que la palabra se rompe,  
hasta que de sus pedazos hago espejos,  
hasta que cada espejo devuelve  
no culpa,  
no vergüenza,  
sino mi cara viva diciendo:

Aquí estoy.  
I am still here.  
Aquí estamos.

Y no nos callamos.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a raw, confessional monologue contrasting one woman’s intimate experiences with the lives of women working in maquiladoras and brothels near the U.S.–Mexico border.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to think danger was a man not calling back.

That was the scale of my suffering: blue light on the ceiling at two in the morning, my body still smelling of him, rehearsing the small humiliations. How I had asked, *Do you want me?* How he had answered with his hands because his mouth was a coward. How, afterward, I lay beside him and mistook being touched for being known.

I called that loneliness.

Across the border, women wake before dawn and knot their hair beneath fluorescent lights. They stand at maquiladora lines assembling pieces of objects they will never afford—wires, screens, the clean mechanical hearts of other people’s lives. Their fingers swell. Their backs burn. A supervisor watches the bathroom clock.

I had spent whole afternoons deciding whether a lover’s silence meant freedom or rejection.

They count minutes because minutes are wages.

And then there are the women beneath red bulbs and hand-painted signs, women whose names are changed for the night, whose laughter may be armor, or commerce, or sometimes—because no life is only one thing—real laughter. Men cross south carrying dollars and permission. They buy an hour, a performance, a version of tenderness with an agreed-upon ending.

I gave mine away and called it romance.

That sentence embarrasses me. It should. Not because sex given freely is shameful, but because I once believed my wounds made me fluent in every woman’s pain. I thought betrayal was a border we all crossed the same way.

It isn’t.

I could leave the room. I could call a cab. I could refuse a shift I never had to work. Even my recklessness had a safety net: a credit card, a locked door, a mother who would answer.

So what right do I have to place my bed beside their factory floor, their rented room, their walk home through streets where missing posters fade in the sun?

None, perhaps.

Only the obligation not to look away.

The border is full of things assembled for someone else: televisions, car parts, fantasies, women’s bodies, stories. Even grief gets packaged. Even outrage can be exported.

I am confessing because I have used other women’s suffering as a mirror, and mirrors are greedy. They return only the face standing before them.

Tonight I want to break it.

I want to say: their lives are not symbols for my emptiness. The factory worker may love soap operas, hate cilantro, send money to her mother, dream of opening a salon. The woman in the brothel may be trapped, may be choosing among brutal choices, may be saving for school, may be exhausted by strangers imagining they understand her.

And I am a woman who once cried because a man touched me without tenderness, then cried again because he stopped.

Both tears were real.

But they were not the same as hunger. Not the same as a locked gate. Not the same as walking through the desert with your name folded into your shoe in case your body is found.

That is the confession: I wanted intimacy to make me innocent. I wanted my nakedness to count as truth.

It doesn’t.

Truth is what remains when I stop making every wound about me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a feminist prose poem that begins with “I’ve stopped asking: ¿Why?” and explores privilege, abortion, miscarriage, sex work, femicide, and a mother’s idea of what it means to be “lucky.”
counterfactuals.output:
I’ve stopped asking: ¿Why? The question was born bilingual and barefoot, made to cross borders no law would recognize. Instead, I ask who gets a door, a doctor, a witness; who may call a choice her own and who must whisper it into a bloodstained towel. Privilege is a clean room pretending it has no walls. It is the fare home, the day off, the clinic still open; it is being believed when you say this pregnancy will break you, being held when the wanted one leaves your body without a name. Abortion and miscarriage share a hallway but not a verdict: in one room they call her selfish, in the other they call her broken, as if a woman’s grief must prove innocence, as if her womb were public property and every empty cradle required a trial.

Outside, a woman works beneath a red light, selling what the world has always taken for free. She counts bills, exits, condoms, the seconds in a stranger’s temper. Do not make her a symbol before you make her safe. Do not confuse rescue with erasure. Her body is labor, border, testimony; her “no” remains no, even when hunger has negotiated the price of yes.

In the morning another woman’s photograph flowers on a lamppost: daughter, sister, mother, missing until found, found until forgotten. Femicide is not a sudden darkness but a city wired to dim women one by one, then blame the night. Officials misplace files. Newspapers undress the dead. Men ask what she was wearing, where she was walking, why she trusted, why she didn’t. I have stopped asking why she went there. I ask why he believed she belonged to him. I ask who taught the knife its entitlement.

My mother calls me lucky. Lucky because I came home. Lucky because the hand that struck the wall did not strike my face. Lucky because the blood stopped. Lucky because there was a clinic, because there was enough money, because the police wrote down my name without laughing. In her mouth, lucky means the worst thing did not happen, or happened only once, or happened to someone else. It is the small umbrella women inherit in a hurricane.

I want another inheritance. I want luck to mean more than survival: a life not measured against a grave, a choice that needs no apology, work without danger, desire without debt, motherhood without mandate, grief without prosecution. I want my mother to say lucky and mean the world finally loved us without asking what we had done to deserve it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical passage in the voice of a Mexican or Chicana woman reflecting on how women are judged as “atrevida” or “puta,” while other women endure exploitation, bruises, disappearances, and murder.
counterfactuals.output:
They call us *atrevidas* when we speak with our whole mouth, when we walk home beneath the moon as if the street belonged to us, too. *Puta*, they whisper, because a woman’s freedom has always frightened those who profit from her silence.

Meanwhile, other women lower their eyes at the factory gates, counting pesos and bruises. Some cross the desert carrying water, photographs, the names of children. Some vanish between one bus stop and the next. Their mothers search the dust with bare hands, posting faces on walls the wind keeps stripping clean. Their daughters become candles, pink crosses, numbers in a government folder. Their killers become rumors.

What kind of world punishes a woman for daring, yet forgives the hands that exploit her? What kind of world stains her name before it names the man who hurt her?

So I will be *atrevida*. I will wear the word like red thread around my wrist. I will say *puta* until the insult breaks open and releases every sister they tried to bury inside it. I will speak for the bruised, the missing, the murdered—not because they are voiceless, but because too many have made a habit of not listening.

Let them judge. We have survived sharper things than their tongues.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an emotionally intense, fragmented piece about gendered violence in Juárez, weaving English and Spanish together and ending with the narrator bitterly repeating that she is “very lucky.”
counterfactuals.output:
They say the desert keeps what it is given.

Cabello.  
Un arete.  
A pink plastic comb with three teeth missing.

They say the desert is empty, but it is full of names.

Marisela. Claudia. Esmeralda.  
Names painted on black crosses, nombres que la policía pronuncia mal, if they pronounce them at all.

My mother calls before sunset.

¿Dónde estás?  
Who are you with?  
Mándame tu ubicación.  
No te subas con nadie.  
Don’t walk alone.  
Don’t look afraid.

As if fear were perfume. As if men could smell it on my wrists.

In the maquila, the lights bleach us into ghosts. We assemble tiny pieces for machines we will never own, for cities we will never see. At break, we trade warnings instead of gossip.

A white truck.  
A man near the bus stop.  
Otra muchacha que no llegó.  
Another photograph stapled to a pole.

SE BUSCA.

The paper ripples in the hot wind. Her smile keeps smiling.

At night, Juárez becomes a mouth with broken teeth. Neon. Sirens. Dust pressing its tongue against every window. I hold my keys between my fingers because someone said that could save me.

Someone always has advice for the living.

Wear jeans.  
No, don’t wear jeans.  
Take the main road.  
No, the main road is watched.  
Fight.  
Don’t fight.  
Scream fire, not help.  
Pray.

I pray to every woman whose name became evidence.

The police officer asks my sister why she was out so late.

She was coming home from work.

He asks what she was wearing.

Her uniform.

He shrugs as if the city itself has shoulders.

Así es aquí.

That is how it is here.

No. Así lo hicieron. This is how they made it: factory whistle, patrol light, courtroom yawn. A mother holding a photograph until the edges soften. A file misplaced. A body renamed “unknown.” A killer translated into rumor.

My sister comes home.

Three days missing, and she comes home.

She does not tell us everything. She washes her hands until the skin splits. She sleeps with the lamp on. When a truck slows outside, she becomes stone.

The neighbors bring soup and lower their voices.

Qué suerte, they say.

Lucky.

Because she returned.  
Because she breathes.  
Because the wound can hide beneath a sleeve.  
Because there is no cross with her name on it—todavía.

My mother thanks God.

I want to ask which God. The God of search parties? The God of shallow graves? The God who watches mothers walk into the desert carrying water, photographs, and sticks to turn over the earth?

But I say nothing.

I walk to work before dawn. I text when I arrive. I text when I leave. I keep my hair tucked away, my eyes forward, my rage folded small enough to fit beneath my tongue.

They say I should be grateful.

I have not disappeared.  
No me han encontrado muerta.  
No han turned my face into a poster.  
My mother has not learned to identify me by a shoe.

So yes.

I am very lucky.

I am very lucky.

I am very lucky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
